extracted.intended_audience: general readers, theater practitioners, and memoir writers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted norms and practical principles for actors, stage practice, public speaking, and memoir-writing as illustrated by anecdotes about Joseph Jefferson, Carl Schurz, and Henry Watterson. Includes craft guidance (acting, stagecraft, rhetoric) and reflections on what makes memoirs enduring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor self-possession and simulation of emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Before his audience he must be master of himself, holding the situation and his art by the firmest grip. He must simulate, not experience emotion, the effect referable to the seeming, never to the actuality involving the realization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: Jefferson 'broke down' playing Caleb Plummer, turned away to recover and the curtain was rung, spoiling the scene. The guidance is that effective acting requires control and the rendering of a character's feeling without succumbing to real personal emotion. Anti-pattern: allowing real feeling to break performance cadence and ruin the dramatic climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit must exceed salaciousness (avoid 'dirt' exceeding wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: We once agreed between ourselves to draw a line across the salacious stories so much in vogue during our day; the wit must exceed the dirt; where the dirt exceeded the wit we would none of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle for comedic/humorous material and storytelling: comic effect should outweigh any salacious or indecent content. Example: Jefferson and the author mutually refused material where vulgarity surpassed humor. Anti-pattern: using salacity as a substitute for genuine wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaner speech; avoid profanity and coarse language
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleaner speech never fell from the lips of man. I never heard him use a profanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm for public performance and persona: maintain refined language; profanity and coarse speech are to be avoided. Example: Jefferson's public reputation for clean speech contributed to his appeal and dignity as an actor. Implication: restraint in diction is a marker of professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal displays and 'gagging' (no gratuitous interpolation)
rubrics_metrics.description: He shrank from personal displays of every sort. Even in his younger days he rarely 'gagged,' or interpolated, upon the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for stage conduct: do not break character with gratuitous interpolations or personal display; let the play speak. Example: at a dinner when urged to 'give a touch of his mettle' Jefferson sat awkward and blushing—showing his deliberate avoidance of self-display. Anti-pattern: actors who constantly 'gag' or perform off-script for cheap applause risk undermining their art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility, devotion to craft, and responsible stage management
rubrics_metrics.description: He possessed uncommon versatility. ... He was a thorough stage manager, skillful, patient and upright. His company was his family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards for a distinguished theatrical career: cultivate versatility across parts; remain dedicated to art beyond pecuniary reward; manage a company with skill, patience and integrity; treat company members responsibly. Examples: Jefferson's long run with Rip Van Winkle yet later return to parts like Caleb Plummer and Acres; elevating the social/intellectual standing of actors. Scoring note: professional stature is measured by range, consistency, managerial qualities, and moral conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memoirs should offer enduring, substantive content (avoid triviality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Talleyrand ... fixed an interdict of more than fifty years upon the date set for their publication, and when at last the bulky tomes made their appearance, they excited no especial interest. ... Boswell certainly did for Johnson what the thunderous old doctor could not have done for himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for memoir-writing and selection: memoirs that are trivial, gossipy, or delayed without striking substance often fail to interest posterity. To endure, autobiographical writing needs either unique insight, a convincing vindication of contested episodes, substantial narrative interest, or an effective biographer's perspective. Examples: Talleyrand, Beecher, Metternich (neglected); Boswell's life-of-Johnson as a counterexample of what makes a lasting record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt and repurpose material to fit occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: I had a cast-off lecture entitled Money and Morals. ... Why might I not put a head and tail to this--a foreword and a few words in conclusion--and make it meet the purpose and serve the occasion?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance for public speaking and debate: you may successfully rework existing material by framing it appropriately (intro and conclusion) to meet a new occasion or thesis. Example: Watterson adapted 'Money and Morals' to the billed debate with McKinley, added a framing preface and closing, and the result was highly successful; McKinley later said the prepared verbatim gave him nothing to reply to. Anti-pattern: refusing to adapt and rigidly sticking to an ill-fitting text when time or preparation is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inclusive framing and rhetorical devices to engage audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: I am an American, and in America every man who is not a policeman or a dude is a workingman. ... Instead of sticking very closely to the text ... I propose to take a ramble through the highways and byways of life and thought in our beloved country and to cast a balance if I can from an American point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical standard for speeches and humorous lectures: open with broad, inclusive claims and anecdotes to align with and win over a mixed audience; then weave in your substantive material. Example: Watterson's opening to the debate reframed the assigned question into an expansive, audience-friendly narrative, which prepared the crowd for the repurposed lecture material. Scoring note: effectiveness measured by audience response and ability to reframe contentious topics into common-ground appeals.
